strengths: Significance: Redundant shared-prefix computation is a useful target for improving RL post-training efficiency. Combining prefix reuse with bounded activation storage could make long, branching agent trajectories substantially cheaper to train.

Originality: The combination of DFS-based training execution, incremental graph release, and prefix-aware distributed partitioning offers a potentially useful systems contribution beyond static tree packing.

Evaluation: The paper reports practically meaningful end-to-end speedups of 1.28× and 2.28× for Qwen3-1.7B and 8B under the same eight-GPU budget. Retuning rollout/training GPU allocation for each system is appropriate for evaluating achievable system throughput.

Presentation and component analysis: Figure 1 communicates the intended execution strategy clearly. Experiments cover four model sizes for gradient-computation benchmarks and include ablations of caching, traversal, chunk size, and distributed partitioning.
weaknesses: Soundness—shared-prefix backward computation is underspecified and internally ambiguous. Section 3 promises one backward pass per shared prefix, whereas Section 3.1 describes sequential backward passes with contributions reaching shared nodes once per descendant leaf. Accumulating gradients at cached-state boundaries and deferring a node's backward pass until all descendants finish could support the claim, but the paper does not specify that algorithm. Pseudocode, explicit gradient dependencies, and numerical agreement with dense-training gradients are needed to establish both correctness and avoidance of redundant backward computation.

Soundness—chunked backpropagation leaves a crucial dependency unresolved. Section 3.2 describes backpropagating and freeing a chunk before proceeding to later chunks, although later-token losses depend on earlier tokens' keys and values. The manuscript does not explain how these later gradient contributions reach the earlier parameter computations, which states or adjoints remain live, or when recomputation occurs. Similar noisy reward curves cannot establish exact gradient preservation. This is a central methodological gap rather than a minor implementation omission.

Comparative evidence is insufficient. Tree Training is identified as the closest training method and criticized for memory and scalability limitations, but no direct comparison is provided. The main throughput comparison uses dense training with activation checkpointing, while DTA combines prefix reuse with chunking and its own recomputation. A dense baseline using comparable chunking and memory optimizations would help distinguish the benefit of tree execution from the memory-management strategy.

Significance and generality are overstated relative to the evaluation. All experiments use one benchmark family at a 16K context limit, and end-to-end training covers only two model sizes over approximately 40 steps. There are no reported repeated runs, uncertainty estimates, held-out performance results, or sweeps over prefix-sharing ratios and tree shapes. These omissions limit conclusions about training stability, typical speedups, and workloads with little prefix reuse.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The manuscript omits essential batch sizes, rollout multiplicities, PPO settings, optimizer and precision details, exact chunk-size configurations, model-state sharding, and implementation availability. The token-throughput denominator is not clearly defined for shared versus duplicated tokens. Benchmark naming alternates between τ²-bench and TauBench, while reference [27] identifies τ-bench, leaving the actual benchmark version and setup unclear.

The distributed scheduling claims exceed their justification. Section 4 optimizes unique tree-token count, but attention cost also depends on context depth and execution granularity. No validation shows that this proxy predicts worker runtime. Binary-search partitioning can optimize the fixed contiguous ordering, but this does not establish near-optimality for unrestricted assignment; likewise, the stated duplication bound need not be negligible for highly shared trees.

Presentation and limitations need improvement. The conclusion conflates the 8.31× gradient-computation result with end-to-end gains, which Section 5.2 reports as at most 2.28×. The 'optimal DFS traversal order' is described only through qualitative heuristics. There is no substantive discussion of low-sharing workloads, serialization overhead, or assumptions required for exact reuse. No material research-ethics concern is apparent, but the unresolved correctness and reproducibility issues prevent acceptance.

strengths: Significance: Redundant shared-prefix computation is a relevant bottleneck in agentic RL training. Combining DFS traversal with prefix-aware distributed batching offers a useful systems direction.

Empirical merits: The paper reports 1.28× and 2.28× end-to-end speedups for Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-8B on eight H800 GPUs. Ablations span four model sizes and 2/4/8 training GPUs, examining both throughput and memory. Optimizing rollout/training GPU allocations for each system is appropriate for the end-to-end comparison.

Originality and presentation: The integration of dynamic graph lifetimes, chunked processing, and contiguous DFS partitioning is potentially valuable beyond prefix reuse alone. Figure 1 communicates the execution idea, and Section 4 gives a reasonably clear description of the partitioning procedure.
weaknesses: Soundness—shared-prefix backward computation is insufficiently specified. Section 3 promises one backward computation per shared node, but Section 3.1 describes backward passes for individual branches and repeated gradient contributions to shared prefixes and parameters. Accumulating gradients at a node boundary before one backward pass differs materially from repeatedly backpropagating through that prefix. The manuscript needs explicit scheduling, graph-retention, and gradient-accumulation rules, supported by numerical comparisons against ordinary training. Similar training-reward curves do not establish gradient equivalence.

Soundness—chunked backpropagation leaves a central dependency unresolved. Section 3.2 describes backpropagating and freeing a chunk before continuing forward. Later tokens still depend on earlier tokens' differentiable KV states. The text does not explain how these later gradient contributions reach already released computations, including what is retained or recomputed. Consequently, the claimed combination of exact gradients, bounded memory, and little recomputation overhead is not adequately established.

Originality and comparative evidence: Tree Training [5] is explicitly identified as the closest training method, but it is not experimentally compared. The paper makes strong claims about its memory, efficiency, and scalability limitations without measurements. The ablation called 'Tree' represents the authors' own method and does not resolve this omission. Comparisons with AReaL demonstrate practical acceleration but cannot establish the advantage over existing prefix-sharing training.

Reproducibility: Essential configuration details are missing, including batch and microbatch sizes, rollout multiplicity, prefix-sharing statistics, PPO settings, numerical precision, optimizer-state placement, attention implementation, and chunk sizes used in each experiment. The DFS-order heuristic lacks executable pseudocode, and no implementation artifact is identified. The workload is also inconsistently called τ²-bench and TauBench, while reference [27] names τ-bench.

Evaluation and significance: Evidence comes from one workload and one eight-GPU machine, despite claims about a wide range of RL tasks and large-scale scalability. No controlled variation of prefix overlap, branching structure, or sequence length establishes when DFS helps or loses GPU efficiency. Reward curves cover approximately 40 steps without reported seed variation, uncertainty, or held-out task performance, limiting conclusions about preserved learning behavior.

Performance attribution and presentation: The 8.31× result measures gradient computation and excludes optimizer updates; the measured end-to-end maximum is 2.28×. The conclusion blurs these distinctions. The baseline uses activation checkpointing, while DTA itself describes activation recomputation during chunking, so statements that it avoids such auxiliary techniques need qualification. A matched-memory comparison and explicit accounting of recomputation would clarify the sources of improvement.

Distributed-method claims and limitations: Optimality of the threshold search applies to contiguous partitions in a fixed ordering, not unrestricted tree partitioning. The stated duplication bound does not establish that duplication is negligible, and tree-token count ignores attention depth and execution overhead. These assumptions need validation or explicit qualification. The paper also lacks a substantive discussion of low-sharing workloads and scheduling overhead. No material research-ethics concern is apparent; the rejection is driven by unresolved technical and evidential issues.

strengths: Significance: Eliminating repeated prefix computation is a useful systems objective for multi-turn agent RL. The reported 1.28× and 2.28× end-to-end improvements for Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-8B on eight H800 GPUs would be practically meaningful.

Originality: Combining DFS execution, incremental graph release, and prefix-aware distributed partitioning offers a plausible contribution beyond static tree packing. The contiguous partitioning algorithm is explained clearly and preserves prefix locality.

Evaluation and presentation: The paper includes throughput and memory ablations across four model sizes, distributed experiments with two, four, and eight GPUs, and reward curves against AReaL. Figure 1 provides an accessible illustration of the execution strategy.
weaknesses: Soundness—backward scheduling: The central claim that each shared prefix is differentiated only once is not established. Section 3.1 describes backward passes for individual leaves and repeated gradient contributions through shared nodes, whereas Section 3.2 describes delaying a node’s backward pass until all descendants finish. These can represent materially different implementations. The paper needs explicit graph boundaries and an algorithm showing how adjoints from descendant attention operations and sequence-specific prefix losses accumulate before a single prefix backward pass. No numerical loss or gradient equivalence tests against dense training are reported.

Soundness—chunking: Section 3.2 says chunk activations are backpropagated and freed before subsequent forward computation. Later tokens nevertheless depend on earlier chunks’ keys and values. The manuscript does not explain how their later gradient contributions reach the earlier computations, or precisely when reconstruction occurs. This omission affects the correctness of the claimed exact training acceleration; similar noisy reward curves cannot substitute for a gradient check.

Comparative evidence and originality: Tree Training, the closest training-specific predecessor, is discussed critically but never evaluated. The experimental 'Tree' variant is an ablation of the proposed system, not a demonstrated implementation of that predecessor. Consequently, improvements over ordinary AReaL do not establish the claimed advantage over existing prefix-sharing training. The broad characterization of tree attention as requiring quadratic materialized masks also needs qualification given the optimized approaches discussed in the related work.

Significance and evaluation scope: All experiments use one benchmark family, despite claims about a wide range of RL tasks. Prefix-sharing ratios, tree shapes, trajectory lengths, and rollout group sizes are unreported, making the conditions behind the speedups unclear. There are no low-sharing stress tests or repeated-run uncertainty estimates. The reward curves cover roughly 40 steps and show training reward only, providing limited evidence for preserved learning behavior.

Reproducibility: The manuscript does not provide code or sufficiently complete implementation and experiment specifications. Missing details include PPO hyperparameters, batch and microbatch sizes, precision, optimizer/state sharding, exact chunk settings, the DFS-order heuristic, and the definition of tokens counted in throughput. Benchmark naming alternates between τ²-bench and TauBench while reference [27] identifies τ-bench. These omissions prevent reliable reconstruction of the reported comparisons.

Presentation and limitations: The conclusion describes 8.31× as an end-to-end gain, although Section 5 identifies it with gradient-computation throughput excluding optimizer updates; the maximum reported full-pipeline gain is 2.28×. Claims of avoiding activation recomputation also require reconciliation with the explicitly recomputed chunk activations. The partitioning discussion calls duplication negligible without specifying conditions under which its bound is small, and token count is not validated as a runtime cost model. There is no substantive limitations discussion addressing these dependencies. I identify no material research-ethics concern, but the unresolved correctness and reproducibility issues prevent acceptance.

strengths: Significance: The paper addresses a practical bottleneck in agentic RL: repeated training computation over shared rollout prefixes. On the evaluated high-sharing workload, the reported gains are substantial: up to 8.31× single-worker throughput, 2.28× end-to-end throughput, and over 50% lower peak memory.

Originality: Interleaving forward and backward computation through a DFS traversal offers a useful execution strategy beyond packed tree attention. Combining this with chunked backpropagation and prefix-preserving distributed partitioning constitutes a meaningful systems contribution, even though prefix reuse itself is established.

Soundness: The vanilla traversal has a plausible gradient-accumulation rationale. The DFS-contiguous partitioning algorithm is clearly specified, and its binary-search feasibility procedure appropriately optimizes the stated tree-token cost under a fixed order.

Evaluation and limitations: Experiments cover four model sizes and multiple GPU counts, with component ablations and a rollout/training allocation sweep. Appendix B honestly reports low-sharing cases where DTA is slower, providing useful evidence about its applicability.

Presentation and ethics: The motivation and high-level execution are understandable, with helpful illustrations and pseudocode. No material research-ethics concern is apparent for the described systems contribution.
weaknesses: Soundness—objective preservation is insufficiently validated. Correct shared-prefix gradients are central, but the paper provides neither a detailed derivation for its GRPO objective nor numerical comparisons of losses, parameter gradients, or optimizer updates against dense execution. It does not explain how trajectory-specific advantages, masks, and normalization are accumulated when shared tokens contribute to multiple losses, including sequences collapsed into longer leaves. The roughly 40-step reward curves in Figure 3, without reported multiple seeds or uncertainty, cannot establish gradient equivalence.

Soundness and presentation—the optimized algorithm leaves a material memory-management ambiguity. Algorithm 3, line 18, performs FWD over the entire new suffix; Appendix A defines FWD as constructing its computation graph. POP_BYCHUNK then constructs graphs again for individual chunks. The pseudocode does not specify when the initial full-suffix graph is discarded or how attached losses and cached-state gradients transfer to reconstructed graphs. As written, it does not establish the claimed chunk-bounded graph memory for long suffixes. Explicit graph lifetimes and gradient-buffer operations are needed.

Comparative evidence: The closest training method, Tree Training, is discussed but not directly evaluated. A FlexAttention implementation with a fixed 24K token budget is used as its proxy, without demonstrating comparable optimization or sensitivity to that budget. Moreover, DTA uses chunked execution while the larger dense baselines require activation checkpointing. A dense baseline with comparable chunked memory management would help distinguish prefix-sharing benefits from memory-management benefits. The current results support improvement over the implemented baselines more strongly than over competing training approaches generally.

Reproducibility: Although hardware, model sizes, context length, and some kernel settings are supplied, important details are missing: rollout/group and training batch sizes, optimizer and GRPO settings, precision, parameter/optimizer sharding, software versions, benchmark task selection, and timing repetitions. These are particularly consequential for interpreting single-GPU 14B measurements and asynchronous throughput. The abstract's code-availability statement contains no usable link.

Evaluation scope and reliability: End-to-end evidence is confined to one high-sharing workload and short training runs for two models. No uncertainty estimates or held-out task-quality results are reported. The low-compression experiments appropriately bound the claims, but they provide throughput measurements rather than broader end-to-end validation. Together with the unresolved correctness and reproducibility issues, this prevents a confident acceptance despite the promising systems design.

strengths: Significance: Avoiding repeated prefix computation during RL training is a useful systems problem. On the high-sharing τ²-bench workload, the reported improvements are substantial: up to 8.31× single-worker throughput and 2.28× end-to-end throughput, with reduced activation memory.

Originality: The main contribution is the combination of DFS-based forward/backward scheduling, chunked recomputation, and prefix-aware distributed partitioning. This provides a meaningful execution alternative to materializing a complete packed tree, although prefix reuse itself is established.

Evaluation: The experiments cover four model sizes, multiple GPU counts, dense and sparse baselines, and component ablations. The GPU-allocation sweep in Table 2 appropriately lets both systems optimize their asynchronous pipeline balance.

Presentation and limitations: The motivation and vanilla traversal are clearly explained. Table 3 usefully documents slowdowns under low prefix sharing rather than concealing them. No material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness: Preservation of the training objective is central but insufficiently validated. The manuscript gives an intuitive gradient-accumulation argument, without numerical comparisons of losses, parameter gradients, or optimizer updates against independent-sequence training. Such checks are particularly important for detached KV caches, chunk recomputation, and shared tokens with trajectory-specific GRPO weights. The approximately 40-step reward curves in Figure 3 do not establish gradient equivalence.

Algorithm specification: Algorithm 3 performs a graph-building FWD over the entire new suffix at line 18, then constructs graphs again inside POP_BYCHUNK. It does not specify when the original graph is discarded or how gradients through detached KV anchors are stored and subsequently propagated. This leaves the optimized execution's claimed memory bound and correctness difficult to verify. Appendix A also assumes every rollout terminates at a leaf, whereas the evaluated workload includes rollouts that are prefixes of other rollouts; preservation of their individual losses needs an explicit treatment.

Baseline adequacy: The closest prior training method, Tree Training, is discussed but not directly evaluated. A FlexAttention implementation with a fixed 24K token budget is a useful baseline, but does not establish performance against that method's implementation. The paper attributes gains partly to sparse-kernel inefficiency and forced tree splitting without reporting measured kernel utilization or sensitivity to the sparse packing budget.

Reproducibility: Important settings are missing, including global and microbatch sizes for dense training, rollout group sizes, sequence-length distributions, optimizer and GRPO hyperparameters, numerical precision, parameter/optimizer sharding, software versions, and timing protocols. These materially affect both OOM outcomes and throughput. The manuscript also does not clearly define whether reported tokens/s counts original sequence tokens, unique tree tokens, or generated tokens in each experiment.

Learning-quality evidence: Figures 3–4 report short training-reward traces without multiple seeds, uncertainty estimates, or held-out task-success measurements. Changing rollout/training allocation can change policy staleness, so comparable-looking training rewards alone provide limited support for unchanged learning behavior.

Scope and attribution: The strongest results come from one unusually high-sharing workload with compression 9.43×; Table 3 shows substantial regressions on some lower-sharing settings. This limitation is honestly acknowledged, but broader usefulness remains conditional. Moreover, the headline dense comparison includes benefits from eliminating prefix-contained sequences and reducing checkpointing; the available ablations should be used to distinguish these gains more explicitly from the incremental advantage over an optimized shared-prefix baseline. Overall, the promising systems idea does not yet overcome the correctness-validation and reproducibility gaps.

strengths: Significance: Reducing repeated prefix computation is useful for multi-turn RL workloads. The reported gains are substantial: up to 8.31× single-worker training throughput, over 50% lower peak memory for Qwen3-1.7B, and 1.28×/2.28× end-to-end throughput improvements for 1.7B/8B models.

Originality: The contribution goes beyond prefix packing by combining DFS-based activation lifetimes, deferred shared-prefix backpropagation, chunked execution, and prefix-aware distributed partitioning. This is a meaningful systems distinction from the packed-tree approach discussed in related work.

Soundness: The vanilla traversal has a plausible chain-rule justification, and the DFS-contiguous partitioning algorithm is well motivated under its unique-token cost model. Ablations cover four model sizes, multiple GPU counts, traversal order, chunk size, and scheduling. The GPU-allocation sweep supports comparing separately optimized end-to-end configurations.

Presentation and limitations: The motivation and main execution strategy are understandable. Appendix B candidly reports low-sharing workloads where DTA loses performance, appropriately delimiting its usefulness. No material research-ethics concern is apparent for this systems contribution.
weaknesses: Soundness—gradient preservation is insufficiently validated. The manuscript provides neither numerical loss/gradient comparisons against dense training nor a detailed correctness argument for the optimized execution with detached KV anchors. Appendix A assumes losses occur at leaves, while the evaluated workload includes sequences that are prefixes of other sequences. How their distinct loss weights and masks survive collapsing needs explanation. Similar training-reward curves do not establish objective equivalence.

Technical presentation—Algorithm 3 does not clearly substantiate the claimed execution and memory behavior. Line 18 invokes FWD, defined as constructing a computation graph, over the entire newly visited suffix; POP_BYCHUNK then invokes FWD again before backpropagation. The algorithm does not specify when the first graph is discarded, how attached losses transfer to reconstructed graphs, or how accumulated KV gradients are retained. Taken literally, the full-suffix graph also undermines the stated protection against long-suffix activation memory. These details are central to reproducing the optimized method.

Comparative evidence: The closest prior work, Tree Training, is discussed but not evaluated directly; a FlexAttention implementation with a fixed 24K token budget serves as its proxy. There is no budget/kernel tuning study establishing that this proxy represents a competitive packed-tree baseline. Figure 5 also shows that collapsing contained sequences materially strengthens dense training, so the headline 8.31× gain over Dense+CKPT should be distinguished more clearly from gains over the strongest dense configuration.

Reproducibility: Hardware, model sizes, context length, and several kernel settings are supplied, but essential training details are missing, including rollout/group and batch sizes, optimizer settings, precision, parameter/optimizer sharding, asynchronous staleness settings, and timing repetitions. The abstract's code-availability statement has no usable link in the supplied manuscript. Together with the algorithmic ambiguities, these omissions impede independent verification.

Evaluation scope and uncertainty: End-to-end evidence comprises approximately 40 training steps on one high-sharing benchmark, without multiple seeds, uncertainty estimates, or held-out task performance. This supports a promising throughput result but gives limited evidence for unchanged learning behavior. The acknowledged low-sharing regressions are useful boundary results; the remaining need is stronger validation of the central correctness and learning-preservation claims.
